# Who benefits most?

::: {.lead}
How **sorted partial effects** describe treatment effects beyond their average.
:::

One hour together: around 35–40 minutes of examples and interpretation, with time for discussion throughout.

::: {.session-links}
[Open the presentation](slides.html){.btn .btn-primary}
[Download HTML](presentation.html){.btn .btn-outline-primary download="jcod-sorted-effects.html"}
[Download the PDF](slides.pdf){.btn .btn-outline-primary}
:::
:::

## What we will cover

A short introduction to the method and papers, followed by a public randomized
**colon chemotherapy trial**: does the average reduction in three-year mortality
hide differences between patient profiles?

Short R examples show how to fit an outcome model, predict each profile under
observation and chemotherapy, and calculate absolute risk reductions. We sort
those estimates, compare twelve characteristics in the bottom and top 10%,
and check the ranking in held-out patients. A brief International Stroke Trial
comparison shows why a sorted curve alone is not evidence of a useful ranking.

The HTML presentation has a chapter map and a two-dimensional overview: use **→** to move between chapters, **↓** to explore their examples, **Space** to follow the full story, and **Esc** to see the whole deck.

## Before the session

- **Suggested reading:** Chen, Chernozhukov, Fernández-Val and Luo (2020), [*SortedEffects: Sorted Causal Effects in R*](https://doi.org/10.32614/RJ-2020-006). Start with the introduction and mortgage example.
- **Optional theory:** Chernozhukov, Fernández-Val and Luo (2018), [*The Sorted Effects Method*](https://doi.org/10.3982/ECTA14415).
- **Optional application (suggested):** Bilancini et al. (2022), [*Prosocial behavior in emergencies: Evidence from blood donors recruitment and retention during the COVID-19 pandemic*](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/36327632/). A health-related observational application suggested in the review; source verification is pending in the [evidence notes](docs/evidence.md).

## Explore the example

[Read the colon chemotherapy pilot](colon-pilot.qmd): the full analysis behind
the slides, with three-year mortality, twelve patient characteristics, one fixed
held-out split and missing-baseline sensitivity checks. The ranking is promising
but preliminary. These results do not establish harm from chemotherapy in women
or a new clinical finding.

The sorted-effect confidence bands use native SortedEffects 1.7.0. Classification
inference uses a separately audited, stabilized reconstruction because the native
classification bootstrap failed for these data. The report explains that
distinction and the assumptions behind the estimates.

[Colon R walkthrough](R/colon-walkthrough.R) · [Analysis plan](docs/colon-analysis-plan.md) · [Classification results](results/colon/classification-stabilized.csv) · [Slide figures](scripts/plot-colon-slides.R)

[Read the International Stroke Trial pilot](ist-pilot.qmd): aspirin effects and
a held-out ranking check that did not support the apparent heterogeneity.

The earlier simulated treated/control example remains available as a teaching
resource: [R walkthrough](R/example-walkthrough.R),
[inference script](scripts/example-inference.R),
[example profiles](results/example-profiles.csv) and
[inference notes](docs/example-inference.md). Its data and age/sex patterns are
simulated, not trial findings.

The previous Synthetic Control Methods session is preserved in the repository under `archive/scm-2026/`, including its slides, figures, bibliography and literature.
